lines.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
Read Clue Card One aloud, Nour, so we do not miss a single word.
Card One says: Twenty paces east where cool clear water greets the morning birds.
Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
Wait, Rami—whose paces are we counting, yours or mine?
Good question, because Rami walks like he is chasing a departing bus!
Very funny, Nour; let us walk side by side at a polite normal step.
Five, ten, fifteen... eighteen, nineteen, and twenty paces right to the kerb!
Look ahead—two sparrows are splashing on the rim of the stone fountain!
Thirty years later, the morning birds are still keeping their appointment!
Now look closely at Card One to see what symbol we need to find.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine question word for 'what?'.

examples.trans: What is that sound?
What is written on the sheet, Rami?

meanings.note: Used in the universal morning greeting صباح الخير ('good morning'), answered with صباح النور.

examples.trans: Good morning! How did you sleep today?
The weather is very pleasant this morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: حلوة, plural: حلوين).

examples.trans: The strawberry jam is sweet and tasty.
The sweater looks lovely and warm.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أيام.

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!

meanings.note: The word 'سبت' (el-sabt) means 'Saturday'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شو هالصباح الحلو يوم السبت لمشية كنز بشارع شارع الياسمين!
examples.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
This is سبت.

meanings.note: The word 'مشية' (la-mashyet) means 'for a walk'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شو هالصباح الحلو يوم السبت لمشية كنز بشارع شارع الياسمين!
examples.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
This is مشية.

meanings.note: The word 'كنز' (kanz) means 'treasure'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شو هالصباح الحلو يوم السبت لمشية كنز بشارع شارع الياسمين!
examples.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
This is كنز.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: The word 'الياسمين' (الياسمين) means 'الياسمين'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شو هالصباح الحلو يوم السبت لمشية كنز بشارع شارع الياسمين!
examples.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
This is الياسمين.

meanings.note: Imperative forms with object pronouns give خليكم بحالكم ('stay in your own business') and خلوني بحالي ('leave me in mine').

examples.trans: Let me speak for a bit.
Stay calm, Mariam.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفحص, بيفحص).

examples.trans: Tariq will inspect the cellar right away.
We checked the heater and pipes this morning.

meanings.note: The word 'بوصلة' (bowSlet) means 'compass'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خلينا نفحص بوصلة النحاس بالأول: الشرق بروح دغري باتجاه مخبز الزاوية.
examples.trans: Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
This is بوصلة.

meanings.note: In Jordanian Arabic, نحاس covers both yellow brass and red copper, often placed directly after a noun (مفاتيح نحاس brass keys).

examples.trans: We polished the brass keys in the morning.
The brass pot is old and engraved.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite noun أول means 'first' (أول يوم 'first day'); after a definite noun الأول / الأولى agrees in gender (الصفحة الأولى 'the first page'). Also used adverbially ('first').

examples.trans: Welcome on your first day of work!
Read the first page calmly.

meanings.note: The word 'شرق' (el-sharq) means 'east'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خلينا نفحص بوصلة النحاس بالأول: الشرق بروح دغري باتجاه مخبز الزاوية.
examples.trans: Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
This is شرق.

راح.gloss: to go; be gone (راحت علينا we missed our chance)

meanings.en: to go; be gone (راحت علينا we missed our chance)
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بروح, بيروح).

examples.trans: We missed our chance — he hung up!

examples.text: كل التعب راح مع أول فنجان قهوة.
examples.trans: All the tiredness vanished with the first cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Classic Levantine word (from Turkish doğru) meaning 'straight ahead' in directions.

examples.trans: Turn left and walk straight to the bridge.
Walk straight to the end of the street.

meanings.note: The word 'اتجاه' (b-ittejaah) means 'toward'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خلينا نفحص بوصلة النحاس بالأول: الشرق بروح دغري باتجاه مخبز الزاوية.
examples.trans: Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
This is اتجاه.

meanings.note: The word 'مخبز' (makhbaz) means 'bakery'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خلينا نفحص بوصلة النحاس بالأول: الشرق بروح دغري باتجاه مخبز الزاوية.
examples.trans: Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
This is مخبز.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: زوايا.

examples.trans: The corner shop opens early.
I love the corner pieces of lemon cake.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقرأ, بيقرأ).

examples.trans: I want to read the booking ledger.
Did you read the second page clipped underneath?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: كروت.

examples.text: بعتتله كرت بريد قصير الأسبوع الماضي.
examples.trans: I sent him a short postcard last week.
I recognised his neat handwriting on the card right away.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أدلة.

examples.trans: I bought the Amman travel guide.
The guesthouse is listed in the annual guide.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أصوات.

examples.trans: I heard the sound of rain on the window.
His voice is calm and polite on the phone.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: عالية, plural: عاليين).

examples.trans: What is that loud sound upstairs?
The wooden ceiling is high and sunny.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

عشان.gloss: for; because of; in order to

meanings.en: for; because of; in order to
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'for / because of' (عشان هيك 'that is why') and 'so that'.

examples.trans: That is why the suitcase was heavy!
Are you polishing the lanterns for noon?

meanings.note: Negates verbs and في (ما بعرف 'I don't know', ما في 'there isn't'), and links conjunctions like قبل ما ('before') and بعد ما ('after').

examples.trans: Paper does not lose room names.
Have tea before you head out.

meanings.note: The word 'ضيع' (nDayye3) means 'we miss/lose'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: اقرأي كرت الدليل الأول بصوت عالي يا نور، عشان ما نضيع ولا كلمة.
examples.trans: Read Clue Card One aloud, Nour, so we do not miss a single word.
This is ضيع.

meanings.note: With two pronunciations in context: walla ('or' in choice questions: عالشارع ولا عالساحة؟) and wala ('not even / nor': ولا خدش 'not a single scratch', ولا يهمك 'do not worry at all').

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: كلمات.

examples.trans: She did not say a single word to anyone.
The word thank you warms the heart.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقول, بيقول).

examples.trans: What does clause fourteen say?
He said thank you and hung up!

meanings.note: Numeral 'twenty' (followed by a singular noun in Arabic: عشرين دقيقة 'twenty minutes').

examples.trans: We need twenty eggs for breakfast.
The ring's width is twenty millimetres.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: خطوات.

examples.trans: I heard footsteps on the wooden stairs.
We walked step by step in the rain.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian question word for 'where?'.

examples.trans: Where is the computer, Tariq?
Where should I put the small spoons?

meanings.note: Universal Jordanian/Levantine word for water (feminine!). Before another noun in possession ('water of...'), becomes مية (mayyet): مية الدوش ('shower water'), مية الشتا ('winter water').

examples.trans: Please drink a glass of cold water.
The hot water is working again in the bathroom.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: باردة, plural: باردين).

examples.trans: Here, drink a glass of cold water.
My hands were cold from the rain.

meanings.note: Describes a pure musical note, clear sky (سما صافية), or clear broth.

examples.text: نغمة البيانو طلعت صافية متل المي.
examples.trans: The piano note rang out crystal clear.

examples.text: انشالله تضل السما صافية طول نهار التنين.
examples.trans: Hopefully the sky stays clear all day Monday.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بستقبل, بيستقبل).

examples.trans: Let us go down to welcome the new guest.
They welcomed us with a smile and hot tea.

meanings.note: The word 'طير' (Tyoor) means 'birds'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: الكرت الأول بقول: عشرين خطوة للشرق وين المي الباردة الصافية بتستقبل طيور الصبح.
examples.trans: Card One says: Twenty paces east where cool clear water greets the morning birds.
This is طير.

meanings.note: Everyday spoken Jordanian noun for 'the morning' (الصبح in the morning, كل صبح every morning).

examples.trans: I drink black coffee every morning.
The morning bread is still hot.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: بسيطة, plural: بسيطين).

examples.trans: Explain the matter to me in simple words.
The problem is minor and easy to fix.

meanings.note: The word 'هادا' (haada) means 'this'. It is a common pron in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بسيطة! هادا نافورة الحجر المنحوتة الصغيرة بآخر الشارع تبعنا!
examples.trans: Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
This is هادا.

meanings.note: The word 'نافورة' (nafooret) means 'fountain'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بسيطة! هادا نافورة الحجر المنحوتة الصغيرة بآخر الشارع تبعنا!
examples.trans: Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
This is نافورة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حجار.

examples.trans: Old stone holds warmth.
She stepped onto the stone step outside.

meanings.note: The word 'منحوت' (el-manHoote) means 'carved'. It is a common adj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بسيطة! هادا نافورة الحجر المنحوتة الصغيرة بآخر الشارع تبعنا!
examples.trans: Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
This is منحوت.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: صغيرة, plural: صغار).

examples.trans: We found a little wooden train in the bag.
There are two small streets on the left.

meanings.note: Placed directly before an indefinite noun without ال- to mean 'the last' (آخر يوم 'the last day', آخر الساحة 'the far end of the courtyard').

examples.trans: The attic room is at the end of the floor.
Today is the last day of the week.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian possessive word ('belonging to'); agrees in gender: تبع (m.), تبعت (f.), تبعون (pl.).

examples.text: اليوم آخر يوم بأسبوع التجربة تبعك.
examples.trans: Today is the last day of your trial week.
My brother's piano teacher!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بستنى, بيستنى).

examples.trans: Wait a moment, I have an idea!
The suitcase is still waiting for its owner.

meanings.note: The word 'رامي—خطوات' (رامي—خطوات) means 'رامي—خطوات'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: استنى يا رامي—خطوات مين عم نعد، خطواتك ولا خطواتي؟
examples.trans: Wait, Rami—whose paces are we counting, yours or mine?
This is رامي—خطوات.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian question word for 'who?' (لمين 'whose? / for whom?').

examples.trans: Who left this envelope here?
Whose is this brown leather notebook?

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: The word 'عد' (n3edd) means 'we count'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: استنى يا رامي—خطوات مين عم نعد، خطواتك ولا خطواتي؟
examples.trans: Wait, Rami—whose paces are we counting, yours or mine?
This is عد.

meanings.note: Often used as a cognate object with سأل (سألتك سؤال 'she asked you a question').

examples.trans: I have just one question.
The question was very easy.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes in spoken Jordanian: لأني (because I), لأنك (because you), لأنه (because he/it — also general 'because'), لأنكم (because you pl.).

examples.text: لأنه القهوة الطيبة بتخلي الناس لطاف!
examples.trans: Because good coffee makes people pleasant!
Thank you because you kept the bag safe.

meanings.note: The word 'رامي' (رامي) means 'رامي'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: سؤال حلو، لأنه رامي بيمشي كأنه عم يلحق باص رايح!
examples.trans: Good question, because Rami walks like he is chasing a departing bus!
This is رامي.

meanings.note: Common defective verb for walking on foot or things running smoothly.

examples.text: ممنوع تمشي عكاحلك لحد بكرا الصبح.
examples.trans: You mustn't walk on your ankle until tomorrow morning.

examples.text: مشينا عالهدا بالساحة بعد ما وقفت المطر.
examples.trans: We walked gently across the courtyard after the rain stopped.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes: كأنها ('as if it'), كأنهم ('as if they').

examples.text: بتحكي مع الجيران كأنهم صحاب زمان.
examples.trans: She talks with the neighbours as if they were old friends.
It sounded as if it came from the heating pipe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بلحق, بيلحق).

examples.trans: Follow me quickly to the third floor!

examples.text: لحقنا دكان الخردوات أول ما فتح.
examples.trans: We caught the hardware shop right as it opened.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: باصات.

examples.trans: The bus station is close to here.
The bus trip was comfortable.

meanings.note: Active participle of راح ('to go'), used like a present progressive in Levantine ('am/is/are going').

examples.text: أنا وسلمى رايحين عالسوق نجيب ليمون.
examples.trans: Salma and I are heading to the market to get lemons.

examples.text: وين رايح بهالسلة الكبيرة يا زياد؟
examples.trans: Where are you heading with that big basket, Ziad?

meanings.note: Placed AFTER the adjective or verb it intensifies: تقيلة كتير ('very heavy'), شكرا كتير ('thank you very much').

examples.trans: The smell is so good!
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: The word 'مضحك' (muDHek) means 'funny'. It is a common adj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: كتير مضحك يا نور؛ خلينا نمشي جنب بعض بخطوة عادية ومهذبة.
examples.trans: Very funny, Nour; let us walk side by side at a polite normal step.
This is مضحك.

meanings.note: Everyday word for 'next to, beside'.

examples.trans: Put a napkin beside every cup.
There is no light beside the bed.

meanings.note: After a plural verb, بعض means 'each other' (بننادي بعض 'we call each other').

examples.trans: We call each other by first name here.

examples.text: ما حكينا مع بعض من زمان.
examples.trans: We have not spoken with each other in a long time.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: عادية, plural: عاديين).

examples.trans: Bread with jam needs regular unsalted butter.
A quiet, ordinary day in the courtyard.

meanings.note: The word 'مهذب' (w-mhadhdhabe) means 'and polite'. It is a common adj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: كتير مضحك يا نور؛ خلينا نمشي جنب بعض بخطوة عادية ومهذبة.
examples.trans: Very funny, Nour; let us walk side by side at a polite normal step.
This is مهذب.

meanings.note: Numeral 'five'; short form خمس (khams) before a plural noun (خمس دقايق 'five minutes').

examples.trans: It is five to twelve.

examples.text: الدكان على بعد خمس دقايق مشي.
examples.trans: The shop is five minutes' walk away.

meanings.note: Numeral 'ten'; short form عشر ('ashar) before a plural noun (عشر دقايق 'ten minutes').

examples.trans: You arrived ten minutes early.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: The word 'خمسطعش' (khamsTa3sh) means 'fifteen'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خمسة، عشرة، خمسطعش... ثمنطعش، تسعطعش، وعشرين خطوة عالرصيف بالزبط!
examples.trans: Five, ten, fifteen... eighteen, nineteen, and twenty paces right to the kerb!
This is خمسطعش.

meanings.note: The word 'ثمنطعش' (thamanTa3sh) means 'eighteen'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خمسة، عشرة، خمسطعش... ثمنطعش، تسعطعش، وعشرين خطوة عالرصيف بالزبط!
examples.trans: Five, ten, fifteen... eighteen, nineteen, and twenty paces right to the kerb!
This is ثمنطعش.

meanings.note: The word 'تسعطعش' (tisa3Ta3sh) means 'nineteen'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خمسة، عشرة، خمسطعش... ثمنطعش، تسعطعش، وعشرين خطوة عالرصيف بالزبط!
examples.trans: Five, ten, fifteen... eighteen, nineteen, and twenty paces right to the kerb!
This is تسعطعش.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أرصفة.

examples.trans: The car pulled up beside the pavement.
We walked along the wide sidewalk downtown.

meanings.note: Used almost universally in the Levantine adverbial phrase بالزبط (biz-zabt, 'exactly / right on').

examples.text: هاد هو اللون الأخضر اللي بدنا إياه بالزبط!
examples.trans: That is the exact shade of green we want!

examples.text: وصل السايق عالباب الساعة تنتين بالزبط.
examples.trans: The driver arrived at the gate at two o'clock sharp.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'in front of, before'.

examples.trans: The golden lanterns against the evening sky.
The car is parked in front of the gate.

meanings.note: The word 'طرطش' (yTarTshoo) means 'they splash'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شوفوا قدام—عصفورين عم يطرطشوا على حفة نافورة الحجر!
examples.trans: Look ahead—two sparrows are splashing on the rim of the stone fountain!
This is طرطش.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: The word 'حفة' (Hiffet) means 'rim'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شوفوا قدام—عصفورين عم يطرطشوا على حفة نافورة الحجر!
examples.trans: Look ahead—two sparrows are splashing on the rim of the stone fountain!
This is حفة.

meanings.note: Means 'after' (بعد المطر) and with a future span 'in' (بعد أربعين دقيقة 'in forty minutes').

examples.trans: He arrives in forty minutes.
How lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'thirty'.

examples.trans: They have given us thirty days in the letter.
The bill is thirty-eight dinars.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: سنين.

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
I have not seen him for three years.

meanings.note: The word 'لسه' (lissa) means 'still'. It is a common adv in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بعد تلاتين سنة، طيور الصبح لسه محافظين على موعدهم!
examples.trans: Thirty years later, the morning birds are still keeping their appointment!
This is لسه.

meanings.note: The word 'محافظ' (mHaafZeen) means 'keeping'. It is a common adj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بعد تلاتين سنة، طيور الصبح لسه محافظين على موعدهم!
examples.trans: Thirty years later, the morning birds are still keeping their appointment!
This is محافظ.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مواعيد.

examples.trans: I always appreciate punctuality.

examples.text: عندنا موعد مهم يوم الجمعة الظهر.
examples.trans: We have an important appointment Friday at noon.

meanings.note: The word 'هلق' (hallaq) means 'now'. It is a common adv in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: هلق شوفوا منيح عالكرت الأول عشان نشوف شو الرمز اللي لازم نلاقيه.
examples.trans: Now look closely at Card One to see what symbol we need to find.
This is هلق.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'good' and adverbially 'well' (نمت منيح؟ 'did you sleep well?').

examples.trans: It has a good, comfortable wooden bed.
Did you sleep well under the wooden ceiling?

meanings.note: The word 'رمز' (el-ramz) means 'the symbol'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: هلق شوفوا منيح عالكرت الأول عشان نشوف شو الرمز اللي لازم نلاقيه.
examples.trans: Now look closely at Card One to see what symbol we need to find.
This is رمز.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Jordanian relative pronoun ('who, which, that') for any gender or number.

examples.trans: That is what I want.
The inn that keeps a stranger's bag safe.

meanings.note: Invariant modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (without ب-) to express 'must / have to / need to'.

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everything has to be just right!

meanings.note: The word 'لاقى' (nlaaqeeh) means 'we find it'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: هلق شوفوا منيح عالكرت الأول عشان نشوف شو الرمز اللي لازم نلاقيه.
examples.trans: Now look closely at Card One to see what symbol we need to find.
This is لاقى.

إلى.gloss: to; until (إلى اللقاء see you soon)

meanings.en: to; until (إلى اللقاء see you soon)
meanings.note: Appears in everyday speech inside warm set phrases such as إلى اللقاء! ('until we meet again!').

examples.trans: See you soon, sir!
Goodbye and until next time.

meanings.note: The word 'اللقاء' (اللقاء) means 'اللقاء'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.trans: Goodbye!
This is اللقاء.
